articles.title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy
articles.summary: Jensen Huang also admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and says he will cooperate with a security investigation.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair and said he would cooperate into a security investigation launched by the tech giant By Nathan Williams   and   Zoe Kleinman ,  Technology editor 
- Published 8 November 2026 Updated 39 minutes ago 
US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports its CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. 
The company, one of the most valuable in the world, said its board had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, adding that the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company. 
Separately, Jensen Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. 
US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. 
Jensen Huang said he took "full responsibility" for what he did, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders. 
Nvidia is one of the world's largest companies and seen as central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, and Jensen Huang has been in charge of it for more than 30 years. 
He said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." 
His statement continued: "Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. 
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American." 
A separate statement issued by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort". 
It continued: "The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders. 
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information." 
US President Donald Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged. 
"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country". 
The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. 
Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he now wished he had "acted on the intelligence" at the time, Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." 
China has previously rejected allegations of an espionage operation targeting the Nvidia chief, describing the claims as "groundless speculation" . 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Jensen Huang is a 'fine person' who has done 'an incredible job', says Trump 
Jensen Huang rescued Nvidia from almost going broke on more than one occasion, and he took a punt on AI a long time before the rest of the world did. 
His decision to make Nvidia chips, originally designed for gaming, become the best in the business for AI development, has now paid off in spades and the company is worth trillions. 
This is a big blow for a man who is renowned for being a workaholic, a perfectionist and someone who expects incredibly high standards from his staff. 
Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, is linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed. 
The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. 
Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, providing chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta. 
The microchip manufacturer is worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever. 
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by the New York Times. 
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking". 
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence. 
Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment. 
Last week, members of Congress wrote to Jensen Huang, asking him to appear before them in the light of the reported relationship. 
Three House Republican committee leaders asked the CEO to appear later in the month, to talk about Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" given his reported relationship with Alice Huang. 
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information. 
"The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter said. 
Nvidia's AI chips have been a major focus of the rivalry between the US and China, and Washington has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold. 
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US. 
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

articles.title: He spent $50,000 on Labubus but now the craze is dying
articles.summary: Parent company Pop Mart's revenue has fallen as appetite for the quirky collectible monsters wanes.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Courtesy of Ensito Image caption, 
Ensito, with his custom-made Labubu teeth, posing with a new doll in his collection By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 7 November 2026 
For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable. 
Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more. 
Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market. 
The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases. 
Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say". 
He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events. 
But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now." 
Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies. 
It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment. 
Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year. 
The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%. 
Image source, Reuters 
The rise and fall 
Pop Mart didn't invent blind boxes but its dolls certainly helped to popularise them around the world. 
The sales tactic made collecting feel "nostalgic", evoking the feeling of opening gifts as a child, says marketing professional Katelynn Carlson, who discovered Labubus through social media and now owns 36 of them. 
One of her first Labubus was a rare doll, making the experience "even more exciting", she adds. 
Labubu, which launched in 2019, has been Pop Mart's most successful line of toys . The monsters became fashion statements and were sported by celebrities including Kim Kardashian and Blackpink's Lisa. 
They regularly attracted long queues and became so popular that Pop Mart had to temporarily pull the toys from its UK shops after reports of customers fighting over them. One fan paid more than $150,000 for a human-sized Labubu . 
A key part of the allure was how difficult some Labubu dolls were to find , with fans repeatedly buying blind boxes to get the version they wanted, says National University of Singapore marketing lecturer Samer El Hajjar. 
Image source, Courtesy of Katelynn Carlson Image caption, 
Katelynn Carlson believes blind boxes were an exciting feature of the Labubu craze 
Pop Mart now has 500 shops in more than 30 countries and 2,000 vending machines worldwide. The firm, which listed in Hong Kong in 2020, is worth nearly $24bn and remains one of the world's most valuable toymakers, despite its shares having fallen by more than 50% from last year's peak. 
Investors worry its global success was just a viral moment rather than sustainable growth driven by long-term customer loyalty, El Hajjar says. 
For Ensito, it is clear the dolls' exclusivity helped fuel the craze. 
"Now it doesn't feel that way. I walk into a Pop Mart and there's a whole series of Labubus sitting there," he says. 
Ashley Dudarenok of China research firm ChoZan says that sense of exclusivity faded as Pop Mart ramped up production to meet demand. 
Pop Mart declined to comment on share price moves and did not respond to questions about falling sales. 
Rivals take over 
As the Labubu mania cools, some of its rivals have become more popular. 
Blind box collectables like Sonny Angels - tiny, unclothed cherub-like dolls - and miniature glow-in-the-dark Smiski figurines have been flying off shelves. And you can now find My Little Pony and KPop Demon Hunters in blind boxes too. 
Miniso, founded in the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou, sells a range of blind-boxed Disney and Marvel characters in more than 8,000 shops globally. 
"Consumers aren't particularly concerned about where the brand comes from," Miniso executive Vincent Huang said earlier this year . "They're more focused on the shopping experience - the designs, value for money, and enjoyment." 
Image source, Future Publishing via Getty Images Image caption, 
Pop Mart faces competition from retailers like Miniso 
Experts say one of Pop Mart's biggest challenges is creating enduring characters. 
That's an area where Hello Kitty brand Sanrio, which posted record earnings in the year to March, has a clear advantage, analyst Boustani suggests. 
Pop Mart has invested heavily in ways to grow its brand, including setting up a theme park in Beijing and announcing a Labubu film - following in the footsteps of franchising giants like Disney or Lego, some experts believe. 
But unlike Disney, which sells a story before it sells a toy, Pop Mart is working in reverse, says Dudarenok. "The real test for next year is whether Pop Mart can make people love a character without a celebrity holding it." 
Image source, Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images Image caption, 
Glow-in-the-dark Smiskis are emerging as a competitor to Labubus 
'Now I only buy what I like' 
After spending huge sums on the monsters, collector Ensito says he is now questioning how much time and money people invest in collections each time a new trend comes along. "There's always going to be a trend every year. There's always gonna be something that's gonna be really popular." 
Melbourne-based content creator Lawrence Yu says that after two years of chasing Labubus, he's likely to be "more selective" before adding to his roughly 50 dolls. 
His Labubu shopping and unboxing clips once drew up to a million views but the frenzy has faded and Yu rarely makes videos about them now. "I definitely think the trend has slowed down... People go crazy and then it fizzles." 
Clara Barbero from Canada believes Labubus are a "dead trend" but is still keeping an eye out for interesting releases. 
"I’m curating my collection more and only buying what I see myself liking for the next few years, and not just buying the newest series that’s out." 
Image source, Courtesy of Lawrence Yu Image caption, 
Lawrence Yu says he has spent about $1,400 on Labubu dolls 
But the fluffy monsters still have truly devoted fans. 
Hedy Khaled from Liverpool says although the hype around the dolls is cooling, she is just as attached to her collection of 70 Pop Mart figurines. 
There's a distinction between those who chase trends and "real fans", she argues, so falling sales do not necessarily mean Labubus have lost their appeal. 
For Carlson says it is the happiness the dolls bring, not the viral trend, that keeps her collecting. She still gets excited about new Pop Mart releases, like its recent cat-themed Labubu series, which has become one of her favourites. 
"I think there's something special about embracing our inner child and enjoying things simply because they make us happy."

articles.title: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
articles.summary: Wong, 30, is among hundreds of Hongkongers detained under the controversial national security law.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Hong Kong pro-democracy advocate Joshua Wong jailed for 10 years By Abel U ,  BBC Chinese ,  Reporting from Hong Kong   and   Kelly Ng 
- Published 5 November 2026 
Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law. 
Wong is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control. 
Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy. 
Having already spent the last six years in jail, Wong, who was due to be freed in January, will now spend another decade behind bars. 
- 
Silenced and erased, Hong Kong's decade of protest is now a defiant memory 
- Published 30 November 2024 
- 
What a defiant mogul's trial says about Hong Kong 
- Published 18 December 2023 
Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was in his early teens. 
On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances. 
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing. 
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence. 
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, to which he pleaded guilty in September. 
Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday. 
Prosecutors said Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing. 
These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard. 
Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party. 
On Thursday, Hong Kong's chief executive John Lee said Wong and Law were "among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong's prosperity and stability". 
Their actions "not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security, and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the general public and the stability of society," Lee said in a statement issued after the ruling. 
Beijing's foreign ministry said China "firmly supports [Hong Kong] in safeguarding national security in accordance with the law". It also called on "relevant parties" to "earnestly respect China's sovereignty and Hong Kong's legal system". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Wong's (left) activism started when he was just 14 
Wong's friend and fellow activist Frances Hui, now based in the US, said she was "heartbroken" and "outraged" by the verdict. 
"Today's sentencing is not just about Joshua. It is part of a broader political crackdown that seeks to rewrite a chapter of Hong Kong's history and erase the contributions of an entire generation who believed they could shape the future of their city," she told the BBC. 
The UK said the sentencing was "a clear example of how the National Security Law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation". In a statement shared with the BBC, a UK government spokesperson called for "an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions" of individuals charged under the NSL. 
According to the US consulate in Hong Kong, the sentencing showed Beijing "will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms" in the Chinese territory. 
Human Rights Watch described the sentence as "cruel and unjust". 
"To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders," said its Asia director Elaine Pearson. 
The harshest sentence under the controversial national security law (NSL) thus far has been handed to 78-year-old former media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who was jailed for 20 years , also after having been found guilty of colluding with foreign forces. 
Who is Joshua Wong? 
Born to IT professional Roger and homemaker Grace in October 1996, Wong was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, which made him struggle with school. 
However, he was quick to challenge established rules and norms when they didn't make sense. In secondary school, he rallied with his classmates to protest against the high prices of canteen lunches on Facebook. 
In 2011, Wong, then 14, co-founded the pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism, which quickly grew in size and influence. 
The following year, the group rallied more than 100,000 people to protest against Hong Kong's plans to implement mandatory "patriotic education" in schools, forcing the authorities to back down. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
At 30, Wong has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism 
By 2014, Wong, who was then at the forefront of a civil disobedience movement known as the "Umbrella Movement", had already become one of the most recognisable faces among Hong Kong's pro-democracy activists. 
In 2016, he co-founded Demosisto with Nathan Law and Agnes Chow, activists who are now based overseas. 
But he often expressed discomfort at being labelled a "protest leader". 
"We have a lot of facilitators in this movement and I'm one of them... Instead of having a top-down command, we now have a bottom-up command hub," Wong told The Financial Times in November 2019. 
Demosisto disbanded in 2020, the year Beijing introduced the NSL in Hong Kong. 
Law left for the UK and continued his advocacy abroad, while Wong stayed on in Hong Kong and tried to run for a seat in its legislature – but was barred, with authorities citing his opposition to the NSL as one of the reasons. 
Meanwhile, the court cases against Wong were stacking up. 
On 23 November 2020, he pleaded guilty to several charges related to his involvement in protests outside the Hong Kong police headquarters in 2019. 
Then came the NSL charges. While still in prison in February 2021, Wong was among 47 people charged with "conspiracy to commit subversion". The group became known as the Hong Kong 47 and remains the largest prosecution so far under the NSL. 
Wong was still serving his 56-month sentence for the subversion conviction when he was charged with collusion under the NSL last year. 
On 22 November 2020, the day before he pleaded guilty to the protest charges, Wong wrote in a post on Instagram addressed to "the people of Hong Kong": "To be honest, I have never had much faith in Hong Kong's politics, but I have every confidence in the people of Hong Kong. 
"Even as political power now poses a comprehensive challenge to the resilience of our civil society, I believe the people of Hong Kong will, as always, find a way to see things through." 
Additional reporting by Martin Yip

articles.title: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
articles.summary: Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state".
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Au was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state" By Kelly Ng   and   Abel U ,  BBC Chinese ,  Reporting from Macau 
- Published 6 November 2026 
Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case. 
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences. 
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au". 
Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party. 
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors. 
Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state". 
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim. 
Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality. 
He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security". 
Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court. 
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison. 
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday. 
Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists. 
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing. 
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020. 
Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail . Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

articles.title: Iran executes three men for 'armed unrest' after January protests
articles.summary: It is claimed Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were part of anti-government protests earlier this year.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Collect Image caption, 
Reza Zanganeh was one of the three men executed in Iran By Olivia Ireland 
- Published 8 November 2026 
Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media. 
Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim , external reported. 
The executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of having ties to Israel and the United States. 
The number of executions in Iran has increased since US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic began in late February. 
The protest movement initially sparked in December last year by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 of January. 
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the US and Israel. 
However foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures and the BBC received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters. 
Tasnim reported that the three men were executed after the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups". 
The damage allegedly included an electricity substation in Karaj which caused power outages in some areas. 
Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence. 
Ten others accused of taking part in the unrest under his supervision were later arrested. 
Reuters news agency reports that they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years. 
The latest executions in Iran come after the UN human rights chief Volker Türk said he was alarmed by the rise in death penalties . 
In August, Türk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests. 
Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International. 
The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.

articles.title: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
articles.summary: For some tourists, the contrast between Somalia's reputation and what they experience on the ground can be striking.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Somalia has the longest coastline in mainland Africa By Fardowsa Hanshi BBC Somali 
- Published 7 November 2026 
As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu. 
This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital. 
Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture. 
Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes. 
"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old. 
The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara. 
But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers. 
Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea. 
Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity. 
"Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says. 
At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species. 
Image source, Mohamud Abdisamad/BBC Image caption, 
Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader wants visitors to experience the "beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu" 
Guiding tours runs in Sucdi's family. Her father worked in the profession for over three decades, taking journalists, photographers and visitors from different countries around Somalia. 
He introduced her to the business nearly three years ago. 
"I started this job as a hobby, but it has become something that I like and am passionate about," she says. 
She now works alongside her father and a team of guides, building on his experience while using social media to reach a wider audience. 
She shares videos of her tours on TikTok, offering people outside Somalia a glimpse of places they may never have imagined visiting. 
She is also considering producing content in English to reach audiences who do not speak Somali. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
A wide variety of fish are available in Mogadishu's markets 
Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu. 
The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow. 
However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security. 
Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down. 
But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation. 
Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital. 
Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life. 
About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department. 
Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city. 
But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Lido beach is one of the most popular places for people to relax in Mogadishu 
"What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says. 
Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue. 
She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen. 
"I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says. 
Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden. 
Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade. 
Image source, Mohamud Abdisamad/BBC Image caption, 
Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub 
For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking. 
American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice. 
His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media. 
"I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says. 
What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere. 
"It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says. 
Image source, Mohamud Abdisamad/BBC Image caption, 
The sand dunes near Mogadishu remind some visitors of the Sahara Desert 
During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes. 
"The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says. 
Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage. 
"If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines." 
But visiting the country challenged those perceptions. 
"Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says. 
Image source, Mohamud Abdisamad/BBC Image caption, 
Romanian Mihaela Patap says she prefers to visit new countries without preconceived ideas 
Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia's natural beauty. 
Although she has spent only a few hours in Mogadishu, she has already visited the sand dunes and taken in the Indian Ocean coastline. 
"The desert was so beautiful to see. I have also enjoyed the beach, and the ocean. It is inspiring," she says. 
Having travelled to Somalia from neighbouring Ethiopia, she says she has been struck by the people's friendliness. 
"I don't see anything dangerous. I feel safe and the people are warm," she says. 
An experienced traveller, Mihaela says she prefers to visit new countries without having preconceived ideas. 
"I travel the world to see new places, to see countries, to see the differences. I don't take a picture in my mind to compare the reality with. I'm just expecting the new to come to me," she says. 
She hopes to share her experience and encourage others to visit Somalia. 
"I'm going to post my pictures and say good things about what I'm experiencing. I'm going to promote it," she says. 
For Sucdi, that potential is personal. 
She is continuing a family profession while building a business in an industry with few women and using digital platforms to reach audiences far beyond Mogadishu. 
"Somalia still has a long way to go before tourism becomes a major industry," she says. 
"Through my tours, I am giving visitors an opportunity to experience its landscapes, our culture and people beyond the familiar negative headlines." 
For her, every visitor is another opportunity to tell a fuller story of Mogadishu.
